o: Pick four distinct words as top/left/right/bottom so the four corner letters agree: top[0]=left[0], top[3]=right[0], bottom[0]=left[3], bottom[3]=right[3]. With at most 15 words there are only 15·14·13·12 ≈ 33k ordered quadruples, so exhaustive enumeration with a distinctness check is instant. Results are collected and sorted by the (top,left,right,bottom) tuple.
k: Search space is tiny (≤ 32,760 ordered quadruples) — brute force is optimal here.
Indexing words by first/last letter can prune, but plain nested loops already suffice.

a.i: Four nested loops over distinct indices test the corner equalities; collect valid tuples and sort.
s: Loop indices a, b, c, d all distinct (top, left, right, bottom).
a.t: O(n⁴) quadruples with O(1) checks — ≤ ~33k iterations for n = 15

w: Exhaustive enumeration is genuinely the right tool at these sizes; mention letter-bucket indexing (group by first/last char) as a scaling idea. Pitfalls: enforcing distinctness of indices (words are distinct so index-distinctness suffices), and getting the sort comparator right in JavaScript (compare element-wise, not joined strings with default collation quirks). Follow-up: generalize to k×k squares with full column constraints (trie + backtracking).
